pr.title: Add some more specific checks to the MIR validator
pr.description:
None of the `PointerCoercion`s had any checks, so while there's probably more that could be done here, hopefully these are better than the previous nothing.

r? mir
pr.author: scottmcm

processing.reason: PR #125851 changes only `compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/validate.rs`: the MIR validator replaces a blanket acceptance of `CastKind::PointerCoercion(_)` and a shared `FnPtrToPtr | PtrToPtr` predicate with per-`CastKind` operand/target shape checks. This changes validator acceptance/rejection of malformed MIR, not the runtime semantics or code generated for any valid program. The frozen analysis itself states the relevant test is validator acceptance/rejection, not code generation output. There is therefore no source-grounded transformation that makes two defined, Miri-clean Rust executions produce different values: the pre-patch and post-patch compiler agree on all valid MIR, while the malformed MIR targeted by the new diagnostics cannot be exercised through ordinary source under the fixed modern compiler. Modeling the validator as hand-written pure Rust functions returning an acceptance boolean would not encode an actual historical wrong compiler transformation and would violate the instruction not to manufacture an unrelated rewrite just to obtain a difference. No counterexample pair can be validated.

analysis.originalLogic: In the MIR `TypeChecker` visitor, cast checking treated all `CastKind::PointerCoercion(_)` variants as unvalidated: `CastKind::PointerWithExposedProvenance | CastKind::PointerExposeProvenance | CastKind::PointerCoercion(_) => {}`. Separately, `CastKind::FnPtrToPtr` and `CastKind::PtrToPtr` shared one loose test, `if !(op_ty.is_any_ptr() && target_type.is_unsafe_ptr())`, so any pointer-like operand could be accepted for either cast kind.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect behavior was a validator transformation that accepted a cast as valid merely because its `CastKind` was pointer-related, without checking the cast-kind-specific operand and target type shapes. This allowed `PointerCoercion::ReifyFnPointer`, `UnsafeFnPointer`, `ClosureFnPointer`, `MutToConstPointer`, and `ArrayToPointer` casts with wrong operand/target kinds, and allowed the shared FnPtrToPtr/PtrToPtr check to accept e.g. a non-`FnPtr` input for `FnPtrToPtr` or a non-raw-pointer input for `PtrToPtr`. The corrected validator decomposes these into per-variant checks with `check_kinds!` on `op_ty` and `target_type`.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR cast expressions/statements represented by `op_ty`, `target_type`, and a `CastKind`; specifically `CastKind::PointerCoercion(PointerCoercion::{ReifyFnPointer, UnsafeFnPointer, ClosureFnPointer, MutToConstPointer, ArrayToPointer, Unsize})`, `CastKind::FnPtrToPtr`, and `CastKind::PtrToPtr`. The relevant domains are `ty::FnDef`, `ty::FnPtr`, `ty::Closure`, `ty::RawPtr(_, Mutability)`, and the broad `CoerceUnsized` types reached by `Unsize`.
analysis.summary: MIR validator casts must be checked per `CastKind`, not by a blanket pointer predicate. The PR replaces the unvalidated `PointerCoercion(_)` arm with variant-specific operand/target kind checks and splits `FnPtrToPtr` from `PtrToPtr`; `Unsize` deliberately remains unchecked because it covers all `CoerceUnsized` types.
analysis.trigger: A MIR body contains a cast whose `CastKind` is a `PointerCoercion` variant, `FnPtrToPtr`, or `PtrToPtr`, but the operand or target type does not have the kind required by that cast variant (for example, `ReifyFnPointer` without a `FnDef` operand, `MutToConstPointer` without raw mut-to-raw const pointers, or `PtrToPtr` with a non-raw-pointer input).
preconditions: The MIR validator/TypeChecker is running over a cast and has both `op_ty` and `target_type` available.
The cast is tagged as one of the pointer-related `CastKind`s rather than an unrelated numeric or aggregate cast.
The test targets validator acceptance/rejection of MIR, not code generation output.
pitfalls: Do not keep the old combined `FnPtrToPtr | PtrToPtr` check: `FnPtrToPtr` requires an input `ty::FnPtr(..)` and a raw-pointer target, whereas `PtrToPtr` requires raw pointers on both sides.
Do not validate `PointerCoercion::Unsize` as an ordinary pointer cast; the patch notes it is used for all `CoerceUnsized` types, not just pointers/references, so it is hard to check.
`MutToConstPointer` needs raw `Mut` input and raw `Not` output; the check does not yet enforce identical pointee types (`// FIXME: check same pointee?`).

`ReifyFnPointer` should be `FnDef` to `FnPtr`, `UnsafeFnPointer` should be `FnPtr` to `FnPtr`, and `ClosureFnPointer` should be `Closure` to `FnPtr`; signature/safety/capture compatibility remains a FIXME.
`ArrayToPointer` checks only that both sides are raw pointers; pointee compatibility is not checked (`// FIXME: Check pointee types`).
`PointerWithExposedProvenance` and `PointerExposeProvenance` are still grouped into an empty arm, so they are outside this fix's coverage.
analysis.testStrategy: Construct two MIR inputs that differ only in the cast's operand or target type for the same `CastKind`: one satisfying the required shape (e.g. `FnDef -> FnPtr` for `ReifyFnPointer`, raw mut -> raw const for `MutToConstPointer`, raw -> raw for `PtrToPtr`) and one violating it (e.g. a raw-pointer operand for `FnPtrToPtr`, or a non-raw input for `PtrToPtr`). Run the MIR validator on both; the valid shape must not produce a validator failure, while the invalid shape must trigger the corresponding `input must be ...`/`output must be ...` diagnostic. Also cover the deliberately unchecked `Unsize` case to avoid asserting a check that the patch does not add. The supplied patch changes only `compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/validate.rs` and adds no regression test, and no compiler was built here.
evidence: None of the `PointerCoercion`s had any checks, so while there's probably more that could be done here, hopefully these are better than the previous nothing.
"CastKind::{kind:?} input must be a fn item, not {:?}",
// FIXME: check safety and signature compatibility.
// FIXME: check safety, captures, and signature compatibility.
// This is used for all `CoerceUnsized` types,
// not just pointers/references, so is hard to check.
input must be a raw pointer, not {:?}
output must be a raw pointer, not {:?}
